title: Manet’s A Bar at the Folies-Bergère
output:
**Orientation**

Stand directly in front of Manet's *A Bar at the Folies-Bergère*, at the centre of the room, and look first at the barmaid's face. From this position, the painting's famous puzzle becomes visible: the mirror behind her shows a customer who should be standing where you are. Step slightly to the right, toward the edge of the frame, and the reflected scene shifts. Only from there do you see the man in the mirror clearly, and the picture's strange geometry starts to make sense.

**The Work**

Manet painted this scene in 1882, and it hung at the Paris Salon that same year. It shows the bar of the Folies-Bergère, a Paris music hall and nightclub. A young woman stands behind a marble counter loaded with bottles, oranges, and a bowl of flowers. Above her, a trapeze artist's green feet hang at the upper left, and a large mirror fills the background, reflecting the crowd in the room.

The mirror is the painting's central trick. The barmaid faces us head-on, but her reflection turns toward a customer on the right, and that man's reflection appears at the picture's right edge. Critics attacked the picture for these inconsistencies, accusing Manet of ignoring perspective. In 2000, the art historian Malcolm Park staged a reconstruction of the scene and showed that Manet's viewpoint was physically possible. The man at the right stands outside your field of view. The conversation the picture seems to suggest is an optical illusion.

The barmaid herself was a real person, known as Suzon, who worked at the Folies-Bergère. Manet posed her in his studio. The oranges are a clue to her status. The art historian Larry L. Ligo notes that Manet often used oranges to signal prostitution, and T. J. Clark argues that the barmaid is presented as both a seller of drinks and a commodity for purchase. Her expression is blank and withdrawn, while her reflection seems to engage with a customer.

**The Artist**

By 1882, Manet was seriously ill. He had suffered from a degenerative condition that would kill him within a year, and this was among the last major pictures he completed. He had spent his career painting modern Paris, its cafés, theatres, and crowds, and he insisted that art should record contemporary life as it was. This painting brings that commitment to its fullest form, combining close observation of a real place with a deliberately unsettling structure.

The work also owed a debt to Velázquez, whose *Las Meninas* uses a mirror to complicate who is looking at whom. Manet adapted that idea to a modern nightclub.

**The Emotional Reading**

The painting holds two things at once: a woman who seems present and a woman who seems far away. Standing in front of it, you can feel the gap between what the mirror shows and what the barmaid's face shows.

title: Van Gogh’s iconic Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear
output:
Welcome to the Gallery at Somerset House. You are about to stand before Van Gogh's iconic Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear. Stand directly in front of the canvas, about two metres back, and look first at the left side of the picture, where the blue fur cap meets the window frame behind the artist's head. From this distance the thick, ridged paint surface resolves into shapes, and you can see how the painting is built.

The work shows Van Gogh in a blue cap with black fur and a green overcoat, his head turned toward us. A white bandage wraps over his head and runs under his chin, covering where his left ear should be. Because he painted the picture looking into a mirror, the bandaged ear appears on the right side of the image, which is why it seems the wrong ear is injured. Behind him hangs an open window, and on the wall is a Japanese woodblock print, Geishas in a Landscape, made by Satō Torakiyo in the 1870s. The print's bold outlines and flat areas of colour show how closely Van Gogh was studying Japanese art when he made this work.

Look at the paint itself. Van Gogh used impasto, a technique of laying paint on so thickly that the brushstrokes and the marks of the knife stand up off the canvas. He admired this method in the work of Adolphe Monticelli, the French painter whose thick surfaces Van Gogh had written about to his brother Theo in 1888. In the background, the strokes are short and directional, which gives the wall and window a restless energy. The cap and coat are built in a similar way, so the surface seems to vibrate under your eyes.

The fur cap has a practical story behind it. Van Gogh had recently bought it to hold his heavy bandage in place and to keep out the January cold. He painted it as a record of the hard conditions in which he was working.

This portrait was made in January 1889, only weeks after the events of 23 December 1888. Van Gogh had moved from Paris to Arles in the south of France, hoping to found a community of artists he called the Studio of the South. He invited Paul Gauguin to join him in the Yellow House he rented there. After a bitter quarrel, Gauguin threatened to leave, and Van Gogh cut off part of his own left ear. He survived, and in the weeks that followed he turned to self-portraits, painting himself again and again while he recovered. This picture, which he described to Theo in a letter of 17 January 1889, is one of the most direct records of that period.

The painting is now in the Courtauld collection. It was in the possession of the colourman Julien Tanguy at the time of Van Gogh's death, and Samuel Courtauld bought it in 1928. Its presence here places it among the Gallery's celebrated Impressionist and Post-Impressionist paintings, alongside Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère.

The painting reveals a man looking steadily at himself while everything around him is unstable. The calm, direct gaze contrasts with the thick, agitated paint that surrounds his face, and that contrast is what holds the viewer.

title: Georges Seurat
output:
Stand in front of the wall to the right of the central window, about two metres back, where the light falls across the canvas. From here the painting's surface begins to break into its component parts: the pale wall reads as a field of thousands of small coloured touches rather than a flat tone. Step closer and the dots dissolve into solid colour again. This is the distance at which Seurat intended the picture to be seen.

This is Georges Seurat's Young Woman Powdering Herself, painted between 1888 and 1890. It is an oil painting, and the whole image is built from small dots of pure colour placed side by side. Seurat did not mix his paints on the palette. He laid down unmixed pigments in tiny strokes and let the viewer's eye blend them. Look at the wall behind the figure. The light and shadow there are modulated by dots of varying density and intensity, so the surface seems to glow without a single area being painted smooth. This method, which Seurat and Paul Signac developed and called divisionism, is the technique usually known as pointillism. The aim was a light that felt scientifically grounded, based on contemporary theories of colour, rather than the loose brushwork of the Impressionists.

The model is Madeleine Knobloch, Seurat's mistress, who bore him two sons. The painting is among the most intimate things he made, and it is a figure study rather than a public scene. A woman at her dressing table, attending to her face, is a subject that appears often in late nineteenth-century Paris, but Seurat treats it with the same rigour he gave to his grand compositions. The stillness is deliberate. Nothing in the room moves, and the figure's concentration keeps the whole composition quiet.

A technical examination added a further layer. A scan carried out by the Italian Institute of Optics showed that the vase of flowers in the upper left corner was originally a reflection of Seurat himself at work. He painted himself into the mirror, then covered that image with the flowers. If the scan is correct, the painting would be the only self-portrait Seurat ever made, and he hid it.

Seurat was twenty-eight or twenty-nine when he worked on this canvas and had only a few years left. He died in March 1891, aged thirty-one, leaving a small body of finished paintings. By 1888 he had already completed A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, the monumental work that made his reputation, and this figure study belongs to the period in which he refined the dot method and turned it toward smaller, domestic subjects. The Courtauld holds it within its wider collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist painting, a group that includes Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère and several works by Cézanne.

What stays with the viewer is the contrast between the method and the moment. The woman is absorbed in an ordinary task, while the surface beneath her is made of thousands of deliberate, measured points of colour, and the mirror in the corner holds a painter who is hidden in the flowers.

title: The Death of Caesar
output:
Stand at the far end of the gallery, where you can see the canvas whole, with the nearest figures in the foreground and the marble-columned architecture receding behind them. From here the composition reads as a single stage, and you can follow the chain of gestures that leads toward Caesar's body.

The Walters Art Museum, however, does not hold this painting. The source material I have describes Vincenzo Camuccini's *The Death of Julius Caesar*, an 1806 canvas depicting the assassination of Caesar, and places it in the National Museum of Capodimonte in Naples, where it has been since 1864. So the work you are looking for is in Italy, not Baltimore. I cannot give you a description of the physical object here at the Walters, because I do not have source material confirming that it is in the collection.

What I can tell you about the painting itself is this. Camuccini painted the scene of the senators closing in on Caesar in the Roman Senate, the moment of the stabbing that the Roman historians of the late republic described. The composition was built around the fallen dictator, with the conspirators' raised daggers forming a tight arc of motion around him. Camuccini was working in Rome, where the neoclassical revival had made scenes from Roman history a serious subject for history painting, and he meant the picture to be read as a lesson in civic virtue and the cost of tyranny.

The painting's history is itself a story of cost. Frederick Hervey, the 4th Earl of Bristol, commissioned it in 1793 and was pleased with the cartoon, a full-scale preparatory drawing, which critics in Rome praised. The first finished version, completed in 1796, was less well received, so Hervey had Camuccini destroy it and begin again. The final version was not completed until 1806. The Earl died in 1803, and his heirs refused to pay for the work, so Camuccini sold it in 1807 to Joachim Murat, the Napoleonic king of Naples. After Murat's fall, Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies acquired it and moved it to the Palazzo Reale in Naples.

For a visitor to the Walters, the connection is the subject, not the object. Both the Walters and Capodimonte collect European art, and the Caesar story gave history painters a stage for the same themes of power, betrayal and republican ideals that run through the Baltimore collection.

title: The Laughing Cavalier
output:
Welcome to the Wallace Collection. Stand in front of Frans Hals's *The Laughing Cavalier*, and position yourself slightly to the left of centre, about two metres back. From there the sitter's gaze seems to meet yours, and the upturned moustache and half-smile sit at eye level. Step closer and the brushwork breaks apart into loose, quick strokes that the distance hides.

*The Laughing Cavalier* is a portrait painted in 1624. The sitter wears a richly embroidered silk costume, and close inspection reveals long, quick brushstrokes working across it. Hals built the image through speed rather than polish. The turning pose and low viewpoint push the embroidered sleeve and lace cuff toward you. The embroidery itself carries emblems. Bees, arrows, flaming cornucopiae, lovers' knots and tongues of fire signify the pleasures and pains of love. An obelisk or pyramid stands for strength, and Mercury's cap and caduceus for fortune. Art historian Seymour Slive called it "one of the most brilliant of all Baroque portraits."

The title is not Hals's. Victorian viewers and the press gave it the name after the painting was shown in 1872 at Bethnal Green, a loan exhibition deliberately sited away from the West End to reach working-class audiences. The sitter is not laughing. He has an enigmatic smile, and the upturned moustache amplifies it. Commissioned portraits rarely showed adults smiling before the late eighteenth century, though Hals often broke that rule, which is part of why his sitters seem to move.

Frans Hals was working in Haarlem in the Dutch Golden Age, painting militia companies, civic groups and individual sitters for a prosperous market. He painted this man at twenty-six, the age inscribed in Latin across the top right corner: *aetatis suae 26, anno 1624*. The sitter's identity is unknown. Nineteenth-century titles mostly called him a military officer, but he may well have been a wealthy civilian. Art historian Pieter Biesboer has suggested the cloth merchant Tieleman Roosterman, who was also painted by Hals.

The painting's own story is a long one. It was sold at The Hague in 1770, bought in 1822 by the Franco-Swiss banker Comte de Pourtalès-Gorgier, and then bid for in Paris in 1865 by the 4th Marquess of Hertford, who paid more than six times the sale estimate.

Look at the eyes. They seem to follow you across the room, because the sitter faces straight forward while the painting stays fixed.

title: A Dance to the Music of Time
output:
Stand in front of the large canvas and look at the group of four dancers in the centre, then move slightly to your left so you can see the bearded figure in the left background, half hidden by a stone herm. From the central viewing point the four figures read as a single ring. From a step to the side, the figures separate, and you can see that the dancer at the back is turned away from us, his face hidden, while the others face forward. That shift in angle is how the painting's sequence of life stages becomes legible.

This is Nicolas Poussin's A Dance to the Music of Time, painted in Rome between about 1634 and 1636. Four figures hold hands and move in a circle. Time, the winged, grey-bearded figure on the right, plays a lyre to keep them in step. Above them, the goddess Aurora runs ahead of the chariot of Apollo, the sun-god, who carries a ring marking the zodiac. The scene is set in early morning, so the dancers are dancing into the day.

The four dancers represent a cycle of human life, and they are also the four seasons. The figure at the back, seen mostly from behind, is Poverty, which in the seasonal reading is Autumn. Next to him is Labour, or Winter, who is wrapped and bent. On the right is Riches, or Spring, and at the front is Pleasure, or Summer, who leads the others. The sequence runs from poverty through labour and wealth to pleasure, and then pleasure leads back to poverty. The painting is a loop, not a ladder.

The work was a commission from Giulio Rospigliosi, a Roman patron who later became Pope Clement IX. The writer Gian Pietro Bellori reports that Rospigliosi dictated the detailed meaning of the scene. Poussin painted it in oil on canvas, using a clear, even light and smooth surfaces, so that the figures seem carved from the same stone as the herm and the classical relief behind them. Scholars still argue about the exact identities. Malcolm Bull traces the imagery to the Greek poet Nonnus, whose description of the seasons Poussin follows closely, and he argues that Rospigliosi may have added the other interpretation after the painting was finished. The bearded figure at the back has been identified as Bacchus, the god of wine, after the scholar Anthony Blunt suggested that the autumn figure was male, a view now generally accepted.

Poussin painted this in Rome, where he had settled to work away from the French court, and he was known for dense, learned compositions drawn from classical sources. This picture belongs to that body of work. Its title did not come from Poussin. A Wallace Collection catalogue of 1913 first gave it the name by which it is now known, and that name later lent itself to Anthony Powell's twelve-novel sequence.

The painting is a meditation on how each life moves through the same stages, with wealth and poverty passing from one to the other. Its calm, measured figures suggest that the cycle is inevitable, and that Time keeps the rhythm for everyone.

title: Madame de Pompadour
output:
Stand facing the portrait from a little to the left of centre, so the light from the gallery windows falls across the canvas rather than glancing off it. From here you can see the way the figure's pale silks and the blue-grey background hold each other up, and the soft, almost powdery finish of the skin. Step closer afterward and you will notice the brushwork dissolving into fine strokes at the edges of the lace.

This is Madame de Pompadour, painted in 1759 by François Boucher, the leading painter of the French Rococo, a style of light colour, curving forms and intimate subject matter that flourished in the courts of eighteenth-century France. Boucher worked in oil on canvas, and in this picture he builds the sitter's luminous complexion from thin, layered glazes and touches of warm pink, so that the face seems lit from within rather than modelled with hard shadows. The composition is deliberately elegant: the figure leans into a sweep of fabric, and the lace and silk are rendered with a shimmering lightness that suits a court portrait meant to project grace and taste.

Pompadour was the mistress of Louis XV and one of the most powerful figures at Versailles, a commoner who shaped royal patronage, politics and the arts. The painting was the last of a series of seven portraits Boucher made of her, which means it closes a long working relationship between painter and sitter. It was first shown at the Château de Versailles, the royal palace where the image was meant to be seen by courtiers, before passing to her brother after her death in 1764.

Boucher was by 1759 at the height of his fame, a favourite of the court and a painter who had shaped the look of the French royal circle for decades. Pompadour had been among his most important patrons since the 1750s, and the series of portraits records how he refined his image of her over time. Painting her for the last time in this polished, luminous manner was a way of setting the final version of her public face.

The portrait leaves a viewer with a sense of composure, of a woman who knew exactly how she wished to be seen. Its surfaces are so smooth and so carefully managed that the painting itself becomes part of the performance of power it was made to carry.

title: Officer and Laughing Girl
output:
Stand at the far right of the Vermeer room, at the edge of the wall where the light from the windows falls across the floor, and look at the woman's face first, then at the officer's hat. From this angle the painting's diagonal opens up: the table, the map, and the figures lock into a single line of depth. Stand closer and the composition flattens into a row of objects; here you can read how the officer's bulk pushes the eye back toward her.

Officer and Laughing Girl, also known as Officer With a Laughing Girl, or in Dutch De Soldaat en het Lachende Meisje, is an oil painting on canvas by Johannes Vermeer, made around 1657. It measures 50.5 by 46 centimeters, a modest size that asks you to come close. The main subject is a woman in a yellow bodice, her face lit by soft light from an open window on the left. Beside her stands a man in a red coat and wide-brimmed hat, his black sash marking him as an officer. Behind them hangs a large wall map, a Willem Blaeu and Balthasar Florisz. van Berckenrode map of Holland and West Friesland, which Vermeer owned and used in three of his paintings.

The painting's most important device is the officer himself. He sits in the immediate foreground, large and dark against the lighter room, a technique called repoussoir, a foreground figure that pushes the rest of the scene into depth. Caravaggio used it often, and Vermeer probably learned it from the followers of Caravaggio. The red of the coat adds a note of power and passion, and the hat is made of beaver pelt, a material prized for keeping out rain and snow. The pelts were imported from the Dutch colony of New Netherland, in what is now the eastern United States, which the Dutch West India Company controlled at the time. So a single hat carries the reach of Dutch trade across the Atlantic.

X-ray photographs reveal that Vermeer first gave the woman a large white collar that would have hidden much of her yellow dress. He later extended her cap to cover all her hair. Both changes pull the eye to her face and expression. The blue apron she wears, mostly lost in shadow under the table, was a common working garment because it hid stains. Art historians read the scene as a soldier's surprise visit during the woman's morning chores. The wine glass in her hand suggests some prosperity, since wine cost more than beer at the time.

Art historians have offered conflicting readings of the encounter. Many see a woman being courted honorably by a soldier. Others point to her open hand and smile as a hint of discreet willingness. The painting does not settle the question, and that ambiguity is part of its pull.

Vermeer was then a young painter in Delft, working in a city that had grown wealthy on trade, and his paintings of this period often turn domestic scenes into quiet questions about status and desire. In 2024 the Frick invited the Indigenous Canadian artist Kent Monkman to respond to this painting in its Cabinet Gallery, with new works that examine how seventeenth-century European art represented global trade and colonization. The beaver hat, the map, and the wine all belong to that same economy.

title: Portrait of Sir Thomas More
output:
Stand in front of Portrait of Sir Thomas More, and position yourself slightly to the right of center, so you see More in three-quarter right half-profile. From this angle the book he holds and the cord knotted in the upper right come into view together, and the fur lining of his coat catches the light against the black satin and red velvet. Look for these details from here, because a straight-on view flattens them.

This is an oak panel painting made in 1527 by Hans Holbein the Younger, the German artist and printmaker who worked in England. The sitter, Thomas More, was an English statesman and humanist, a scholar who championed classical learning and served as a powerful knighted speaker in Parliament. Holbein paints him in a fur-lined coat of rich fabrics, and around his shoulders hangs a livery chain of Tudor Collar of Esses, with Tudor roses linked along it. Such a chain signaled loyalty to the crown and high office. Notice, too, the cord in the upper right, tied in a loose Franciscan knot. It points to More's private spiritual convictions, a quieter counterpart to the public honors on his chest. On his left index finger he wears a wedding ring set with a stone. Holbein renders each of these things with a precision that lets the surfaces of the velvet, satin, and fur read as distinct materials.

Holbein made this portrait in London in 1527, during his first stretch in England, which began around 1526. He had arrived with a letter of introduction, and through the Dutch humanist Desiderius Erasmus he was steered toward More, the man who would become his most important patron there. The painting is a record of that relationship, and of Holbein's ability to make a sitter look both intellectually formidable and personally reserved. The Frick's version is one of several related works. A closely related drawing with bodycolour survives in the Royal Collection, and a later copy hangs in the National Portrait Gallery, London. Another Holbein portrait of More, part of a large family group, is now lost, though drawings and copies of it still exist.

The painting's meaning sits in that tension between worldly rank and inner faith. More's chain announces his public standing, while the knotted cord and the ring speak to the private man. Holbein holds those two registers together in one face, which is why the image still reads as a portrait of a person rather than only of an office.

title: Portrait of Comtesse d'Haussonville
output:
Stand at the center of the room, about six feet back from the canvas, and look for the mirror. Ingres painted the sitter fully frontal, but behind her, in the dresser's glass, a second image of her appears, and from this distance you can see how the reflection repeats the pose and the composition without quite matching it. Up close, the reflection is hard to read. From here, the reversed space becomes legible, and the painting's central trick reveals itself.

Portrait of Comtesse d'Haussonville, painted in 1845 by the French Neoclassical painter Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres, shows Louise de Broglie, a twenty-seven-year-old countess from one of France's wealthiest families. She stands fully facing us in a heavily folded satin dress the cool grey-blue of her own eyes. Her hair is parted, with a crimson ribbon tied at the back. Her raised left index finger rests near her mouth, and her right arm curves in a long, sinuous line that Ingres deliberately stretched beyond natural proportion. The palette stays within pale blue, grey, brown, gold and white, so the crimson ribbon becomes the one sharp accent in the room. On the dresser before the mirror sit writing materials, pots, flowers, and a lavishly decorated oriental vase.

The composition repeats a device Ingres first used in his 1814 Portrait of Madame de Senonnes: the sitter's image caught in a mirror behind her. Here it lets him show her from two angles at once, which is a claim about how she wants to be seen as much as a formal experiment. The finger at the lips, the parted hair, and the direct gaze have been compared to his later portrait of Madame Moitessier, and critics have long read the whole work as a study in poised, guarded intimacy.

Ingres was then the most sought-after portraitist in France, but he regarded portraiture as a lesser calling than history painting, the grand Neoclassical subjects that earned prestige but far less money. He accepted only two portrait commissions at this point, this one and the Portrait of Baronne de Rothschild. Earlier, he had sketched the countess in black chalk and begun an oil version around 1842, then abandoned it. The sessions were long, and she found them tedious. One complaint recorded that for nine days Ingres had been working on a single hand. She became pregnant with her third child and could no longer sit, so the first attempt stayed unfinished, and this 1845 canvas was the result of starting over.

Ingres later grumbled that he had not captured her charms, but her family was delighted. Her father, the duc de Broglie, approved, and the politician Adolphe Thiers teased Ingres that he must have been in love with her to paint her that way. Ingres replied that the compliment did not satisfy him.

The painting was shown in 1846 alongside the Grande Odalisque and the Odalisque with Slave. Charles Baudelaire praised all three for their voluptuousness and called Ingres the quintessential painter of women. Nearby, the Frick's small Cabinet display of hand-colored fashion plates from Gallerie des modes et costumes français, produced in Paris between 1778 and 1787, offers a useful counterpoint: the same silhouettes and satin that the countess's dress deploys in pale grey-blue, rendered for a public eager to see what people were wearing.
